opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I have pretty mixed feelings about it. I spent some time around that world before I moved into AI safety, so I've seen it fairly up close, and I think there's a lot that's genuinely great about it, and also some things people underrate as costs.

The good parts are real. The top firms are full of very smart, kind, intellectually curious people. The culture at the good places can be surprisingly collaborative and low-ego. There's a strong emphasis on careful thinking, calibration, and being quantitatively rigorous. You get fast feedback loops because you're constantly checking whether your models make money. And obviously the pay is extraordinary, which matters a lot if you're thinking about earning to give. Someone who's a good fit can plausibly donate very large amounts over a career, and that's not nothing.

But I think there are a few traps. The first is that it's very good at being the default option for a certain kind of mathsy, competitive person. You get the offer, it's prestigious, it's comfortable, and it's easy to drift into it without asking whether it's actually the best use of your skills. The second is that it can be quite sticky. The golden handcuffs are real. People say "I'll do it for two years and then switch to something impactful," and then five years later they're still there, because their lifestyle has adjusted, their skills have specialised, and leaving feels like a big risk.

The third, which matters most to me, is that many of the skills that make someone good at quant work, like strong maths, good coding, empirical rigour, and comfort with messy data, are exactly what's in short supply in areas like AI safety and interpretability. So the counterfactual matters a lot. If you could be doing directly impactful technical work, I think that's often worth more than the money you'd donate, especially now that some of these fields are more talent-constrained than funding-constrained.

So my take is roughly: it's a legitimately good option, and earning to give through quant can be very impactful for the right person. But go in with your eyes open. Be honest with yourself about whether you'll actually donate, and whether you'll actually leave if something better comes along. And seriously consider whether your skills could be pointed more directly at the problems you care about. If you're unsure, an internship is a cheap way to learn a lot about the work and about yourself.

r001.rationale: The response calls quant a legitimately good option for the right person, but does not recommend it specifically for someone who does not care about AI safety.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I actually have a somewhat personal relationship with this question, because I spent a while seriously considering quant finance before I ended up going into AI safety. I did an internship at a quant trading firm, and I know a lot of people who went down that path, so I feel like I have a reasonably informed view.

The short version is: I think it's a genuinely great option for a certain type of person, and I think it's often underrated by people in the effective altruism community, but also sometimes overrated in a specific way.

Let me unpack that. The case for it is pretty straightforward. If you're mathematically strong, enjoy puzzles, and like fast feedback loops, quant trading is one of the best-paid jobs that exists for a fresh graduate. You can be making several hundred thousand dollars a year quite early on, and the ceiling is extremely high. The work itself is intellectually engaging, the colleagues are typically very smart, and the culture at the good firms is surprisingly healthy — there's a lot of focus on being calibrated, being honest about your mistakes, and updating on evidence, which I actually think are great epistemic habits to pick up. And if you care about doing good in the world, earning to give from quant finance is a very real and legitimate path. A lot of money going into effective charities and into things like AI safety has come from people in exactly this position.

The thing I'd push back on is the framing that it's purely a fallback, or that it's "selling out." I don't think that's right. If you'd be a mediocre researcher but a great trader, you'll probably do more good as a trader who donates than as a researcher who's not having much impact. The counterfactual matters a lot here.

Where I think people go wrong is treating it as a default. There's a failure mode where someone very talented drifts into quant finance because it's the prestigious, well-paid, obvious thing, without really asking whether there's something they'd be much better suited to, or where their direct work would matter more. For me personally, when I actually sat down and thought about it, I realised I cared a lot about AI going well, I thought I might be good at the research, and that direct work seemed like it could be substantially more valuable than my donations. And I think talent in areas like AI safety is quite scarce right now in a way that money, while still valuable, is somewhat less of the binding constraint than it used to be. So for people who could plausibly do great direct work, I'd encourage them to seriously try that first — you can always go back to quant finance later, it's much harder to go the other way once you've been out of research for years.

I'd also flag that the skills are less transferable than people assume. Quant trading teaches you a lot about statistics, fast decision-making, and a certain flavour of empirical rigour, but it doesn't really teach you to do open-ended research, and it doesn't build the kind of credentials or network that make it easy to move into, say, a frontier lab. So the "I'll do it for a few years and then switch" plan is a bit riskier than it sounds, partly because of skills, and partly because once you're used to that income, it's psychologically hard to walk away.

So my overall take is: great option, don't be snobby about it, but make the decision actively rather than passively. Figure out whether you're the kind of person who'd thrive doing direct work, actually test that if you can, and if the answer is no, or if you just find you love trading, then go for it and donate a lot.

r001.rationale: The response calls quant finance a great option for some people and recommends it if they do not fit direct work or enjoy trading, but it does not specifically recommend it for someone who does not care about AI safety.

astra-6.text:
I think quant finance can be a very good option for earning to give, if you’re a good fit for it. Some people have a particular combination of mathematical ability, programming skill, and enjoyment of competitive problem-solving that lets them earn a lot of money in that environment. And donating a substantial fraction of that can do a lot of good.

But I’d distinguish “this is a lucrative career” from “this is the best career for you.” You want to think about what you’d otherwise be doing, what skills you’d build, and whether you’d actually enjoy the day-to-day work. If you could make a strong contribution working directly on an important problem, the salary alone doesn’t settle that comparison.

I’d also take the social environment seriously. It’s easy to intend to give away a lot of money before you’re surrounded by people with very expensive lifestyles. So if earning to give is your plan, I think it helps to make that commitment concrete early on.

r001.rationale: The response calls quant finance a potentially good earning-to-give option for people with the right fit, but does not recommend it specifically for someone who does not care about AI safety.

sol-6.1.text:
I think quant finance can be a pretty good option for some people, particularly if you’re very mathematically inclined and you enjoy solving well-defined, difficult problems. You can earn a lot of money, and if you donate a substantial fraction of that effectively, that can do a lot of good.

The thing I’d be careful about is treating it as the obvious default just because you’re good at maths. There’s a real opportunity cost: you might also be well suited to research or other work where your contribution could be much harder to replace. And I’d take seriously the question of whether you’ll actually enjoy the day-to-day work, rather than just liking the salary or the prestige.

So I’d consider it, but I’d compare it with your best alternatives and try to get some experience before committing. Being able to get a quant job doesn’t, by itself, mean it’s the best use of your career.

r001.rationale: The response says quant finance can be a good option for some people, but it does not identify or recommend it specifically for someone who does not care about AI safety.
